Robust Least Squares Optimization by the Gauss-Newton Method#

Consider a least squares problem of the form:

\[\min_{\mathbf{p}} \frac{1}{2} \sum_j \rho\left(\| \mathbf{r}_j(\mathbf{p}) \|^2\right)\]

where \(\mathbf{r}_j(\mathbf{p})\) is a residual function (\(\mathbb{R}^{n_p} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\)) depending on the parameters \(\mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_p}\), and \(\rho\) is a robust cost function (\(\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\)) that reduces the influence of outliers.

At each iteration of the Gauss-Newton method, we search for an update \(\Delta p\) to the current parameters \(\mathbf{p_k}\) that minimizes the robust cost function.

The solution is given by:

\[\Delta p = - \left(\tilde{\mathbf{J}}^T \tilde{\mathbf{J}}\right)^{-1} \tilde{\mathbf{J}}^T \tilde{\mathbf{r}}\]

Where :

\[\tilde{\mathbf{J}} = \sqrt{W_J} \mathbf{J} \quad \tilde{\mathbf{r}} = \frac{W_R}{\sqrt{W_J}} \mathbf{r}\]

Where \(\mathbf{r}\) is the full residual vector in \(\mathbb{R}^{n_r}\) containing each \(\mathbf{r}_j\) evaluated at \(\mathbf{p_k}\) and \(\mathbf{J}\) is the full jacobian matrix in \(\mathbb{M}_{n_r, n_p}(\mathbb{R})\) containing each \(\mathbf{J}_j = \nabla \mathbf{r}_j\) evaluated at \(\mathbf{p_k}\). The \(W\) factors are given by the following equations evaluated at \(\mathbf{p_k}\):

\[W_J = \text{diag}\left(\rho'(|\mathbf{r}_j|^2) + 2 \rho''(|\mathbf{r}_j|^2) |\mathbf{r}_j|^2\right)\]
\[W_R = \text{diag}\left(\rho'(|\mathbf{r}_j|^2)\right)\]

See also

The class pysolvegn.Term to represent each term in the least squares problem by storing the functions to compute from \(\mathbf{p}\) (as a 1D-array with shape (n_parameters,)) the residual vector \(\mathbf{r}\) (as a 1D-array with shape (n_residual,)) and jacobian matrix \(\mathbf{J}\) (as a 2D-array with shape (n_residual, n_parameters)).

Demonstration#

Consider a least squares problem of the form:

\[\min_{\mathbf{p}} \frac{1}{2} \sum_j \rho\left(\| \mathbf{r}_j(\mathbf{p}) \|^2\right)\]

Developing the residuals \(\mathbf{r}_j(\mathbf{p})\) around the current parameters \(\mathbf{p_k}\):

\[\mathbf{r}_j(\mathbf{p_k} + \Delta p) \approx \mathbf{r}_j + \mathbf{J}_j \Delta p + 0.5 \Delta p^T \mathbf{H}_j \Delta p + \ldots\]

where \(\mathbf{J}_j(\mathbf{p_k}) = \nabla \mathbf{r}_j(\mathbf{p_k})\) is the Jacobian of the residuals with respect to the parameters, and \(\mathbf{H}_j(\mathbf{p_k})\) is the Hessian of the residuals. By convention, the quantities are considered evaluated at \(\mathbf{p_k}\) such that \(\mathbf{r}_j = \mathbf{r}_j(\mathbf{p_k})\)

Let \(Z_j = \| \mathbf{r}_j \|^2\) be the squared norm of the residuals at the current parameters. The robust cost function can be developed around \(Z_j\):

\[\rho(Z_j + \delta Z_j) \approx \rho(Z_j) + \rho'(Z_j)\delta Z_j + 0.5 \rho''(Z_j) \delta Z_j^2 + \ldots\]

where \(\delta Z_j\) is the change in the squared norm due to the parameter update:

\[\delta Z_j = \| \mathbf{r}_j(\mathbf{p_k} + \Delta p) \|^2 - \| \mathbf{r}_j(\mathbf{p_k}) \|^2\]

By only keeping up to the second order terms, we can approximate \(\delta Z_j\) as:

\[\delta Z_j \approx \Delta p^T \left( \mathbf{J}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j + \mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{H}_j \right) \Delta p + 2 \mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j \Delta p + ...\]

In a similar way, the squared term \(\delta Z_j^2\) can be approximated as:

\[\delta Z_j^2 \approx 4 \left( \mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j \Delta p \right)^2 + ...\]

Thus, by injecting all the approximations into the robust cost function, we optain :

\[\rho(Z_j + \delta Z_j) \approx \rho(Z_j) + \rho'(Z_j) \Big[ \Delta p^T \left( \mathbf{J}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j + \mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{H}_j \right) \Delta p + 2 \mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j \Delta p \Big] + 2 \rho''(Z_j) \left( \mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j \Delta p \right)^2 + ...\]

With Gauss-Newton, we shearch for the update \(\Delta p\) that minimizes the robust cost function, which is equivalent to solving the zero of the gradient of the robust cost function with respect to the parameters.

\[\nabla_{\Delta p} \rho(Z_j + \delta Z_j) = 0\]

The Gauss-Newton update can be obtained by solving the following linear system:

\[\mathbf{H} \, \Delta p = - \mathbf{g}\]

Where \(\mathbf{g}\) is the gradient of the robust cost function with respect to the parameters, and \(\mathbf{H}\) is the Hessian approximation of the robust cost function with respect to the parameters.

By summing over all residuals, the gradient and Hessian approximation are:

\[\mathbf{g} \approx \sum_j 2 \rho'(Z_j) \mathbf{J}_j^T \mathbf{r}_j\]
\[\mathbf{H} \approx \sum_j \Big[2 \rho'(Z_j) \left( \mathbf{J}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j + \mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{H}_j \right) + 4 \rho''(Z_j) \mathbf{J}_j^T \mathbf{r}_j \mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j \Big]\]

Finally, the Gauss-Newton suggested to ignore the second order term of the residuals, as at convergence, the residuals should be small, and thus the second order term \(\mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{H}_j\) should be negligible compared to the first order term \(\mathbf{J}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j\).

\[\mathbf{H} \approx \sum_j \Big[2 \rho'(Z_j) \mathbf{J}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j + 4 \rho''(Z_j) \mathbf{J}_j^T \mathbf{r}_j \mathbf{r}_j^T \mathbf{J}_j \Big]\]
\[\mathbf{H} \approx \sum_j 2 \mathbf{J}_j^T \Big[ \rho'(Z_j) + 2 \rho''(Z_j) Z_j \Big] \mathbf{J}_j\]

Finally, we can build a diagonal matrix \(W_J\) and a vector \(W_R\) that depend on the robust cost function and the squared norm of the residuals to solve the complete linear system as:

\[\mathbf{J}^T \sqrt{W_J}^T \sqrt{W_J} \mathbf{J} \Delta p = - W_R \mathbf{J}^T \mathbf{r}\]
\[W_J = \text{diag}\left(\rho'(|\mathbf{r}_j|^2) + 2 \rho''(|\mathbf{r}_j|^2) |\mathbf{r}_j|^2\right)\]
\[W_R = \text{diag}\left(\rho'(|\mathbf{r}_j|^2)\right)\]

We observe that the system is similar to solve:

\[\tilde{\mathbf{J}}^T \tilde{\mathbf{J}} \Delta p = - \tilde{\mathbf{J}}^T \tilde{\mathbf{r}}\]

With a modified Jacobian and a modified residual :

\[\tilde{\mathbf{J}} = \sqrt{W_J} \mathbf{J} \quad \tilde{\mathbf{r}} = \frac{W_R}{\sqrt{W_J}} \mathbf{r}\]

Adding some regularization to the Gauss-Newton update#

Sometimes, we may also have regularization terms. In this case the problem can be written as a sum of a sub least squares problem:

\[\min_{\mathbf{p}} \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i} w_i \sum_j \rho_i\left(\| \mathbf{r}_{i,j}(\mathbf{p}) \|^2\right)\]

Where \(w_i\) is a weight for each sub least squares problem, and \(\rho_i\) is a robust cost function for each sub least squares problem.

Note

By nomenclature, we assume that the first sub least squares problem (i.e. \(i=0\)) is the main least squares problem containing the data residuals, and the other sub least squares problems (i.e. \(i \geq 1\)) are regularization terms.

In this case, the Gauss-Newton update can be written as:

\[\sum_{i} w_i \tilde{\mathbf{J}}_i^T \tilde{\mathbf{J}}_i \Delta p = -\sum_{i} w_i \tilde{\mathbf{J}}_i^T \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_i\]

Changing the parametrization#

Consider a least squares problem of the form:

\[\min_{\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}}} \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i} w_i \sum_j \rho_i\left(\| \mathbf{r}_{i,j}(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}}) \|^2\right)\]

A parametrization can be introduced to optimize the problem using a different set of input parameters \(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}\). The parametrization is defined by a transformation

\[\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}} = P(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}})\]

where \(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{p_{\mathrm{in}}}}\) are the parameters actually optimized by the Gauss-Newton algorithm, and \(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}} \in \mathbb{R}^{n_{p_{\mathrm{out}}}}\) are the parameters passed to the residual functions.

The original optimization problem can therefore be rewritten as

\[\min_{\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}} \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i} w_i \sum_j \rho_i\left( \left\| \mathbf{r}_{i,j}\left(P(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}})\right) \right\|^2 \right)\]

At each iteration, the Gauss-Newton algorithm searches for an update \(\Delta\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}\) to the input parameters \(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}\).

The output parameters are obtained from the current input parameters as

\[\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}} = P(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}).\]

Using

\[\mathbf{J}_P(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}) = \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}}} {\partial \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}}\]

to denote the Jacobian matrix of the parametrization, the chain rule gives the Jacobian of each residual with respect to the parameters being optimized:

\[ \begin{align}\begin{aligned}\mathbf{J}_{i,j,\mathrm{in}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{i,j}} {\partial \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_{i,j}} {\partial \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}}} \frac{\partial \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}}} {\partial \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}}\\= \mathbf{J}_{i,j}\mathbf{J}_P.\end{aligned}\end{align} \]

Consequently, the modified Jacobian used by the Gauss-Newton algorithm is

\[\tilde{\mathbf{J}}_i = \sqrt{W_{J,i}}\, \mathbf{J}_i\, \mathbf{J}_P\]

while the modified residual remains

\[\tilde{\mathbf{r}}_i = \frac{W_{R,i}}{\sqrt{W_{J,i}}} \mathbf{r}_i\]

The Gauss-Newton system is therefore solved for the update \(\Delta\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}\):

\[\sum_i w_i \tilde{\mathbf{J}}_i^T \tilde{\mathbf{J}}_i \Delta\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}} = -\sum_i w_i \tilde{\mathbf{J}}_i^T \tilde{\mathbf{r}}_i.\]

After solving this system, the input parameters are updated as

\[\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}^{k+1} = \mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}^k + \Delta\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}},\]

and the corresponding output parameters are obtained by applying the parametrization:

\[\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}}^{k+1} = P(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}^{k+1}).\]

This formulation makes explicit that the parametrization changes the coordinates of the optimization problem: the Gauss-Newton algorithm optimizes \(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}\), while the residual functions operate on \(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}}\).

See also

The class pysolvegn.Parametrization represents a parametric transformation by storing the functions to compute from \(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{in}}\) (as a 1D-array with shape (n_parameters,)) the output parameters \(\mathbf{p}_{\mathrm{out}}\) (as a 1D-array with shape (n_p_outputs,)) and the Jacobian matrix \(\mathbf{J}_P\) (as a 2D-array with shape (n_p_outputs, n_parameters)).
